```{r}
#| label: shared-data-and-models
#| results: hide
q <- load_quarterly()
panel <- q |>
  filter(qtr <= yearquarter("2019 Q4")) |>
  transmute(quarter = gsub(" ", "", format(qtr)),
            observation_date = as.Date(qtr) + months(2),
            CPIAUCSL = cpi, UNRATE = unrate, TB3MS = tbill, inflation = infl) |>
  as.data.frame()
stopifnot(nrow(panel) == 240, !anyNA(panel), !anyDuplicated(panel$quarter),
          all(diff(as.integer(format(panel$observation_date, "%Y")) * 4 +
                   as.integer(format(panel$observation_date, "%m")) / 3) == 1))
initial <- subset(panel, quarter <= "1999Q4")
stopifnot(nrow(initial) == 160)
series <- c("inflation", "UNRATE", "TB3MS")
series_names <- c("CPI inflation", "Unemployment", "3-month T-bill rate")
```

# Stage 1 recap

For Stage 2 we use the instructor-provided CSVs and the shared data loader.
They match our individual Stage 1 FRED downloads through 2019. The series are
CPIAUCSL, UNRATE, and TB3MS, selecting March, June, September, and December
rather than averaging months. Inflation is
$\pi_t=400\log(P_t/P_{t-1})$, using December 1959 as the base for 1960Q1.
There are 160 complete quarters in 1960Q1-1999Q4 and 240 through 2019Q4,
with no missing or duplicate quarters.

Inflation averages `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(initial$inflation))`%, but is much
higher in the 1970s and early 1980s than at the start or end of the sample.
The Stage 1 trailing summaries and PELT analysis show a changing center and
variability. The number of PELT/BIC breaks depends on the noise assumption: 17
with the default unscaled specification and 6 after scaling by an estimated
noise standard deviation. Both versions place breaks at 1973Q1 and 1981Q4, the
start and end of the high-inflation period. The dates are descriptive, not
confirmed regime boundaries, and do not enter the forecasting regressions below.
The inflation-unemployment correlation is
`r sprintf("%.2f", cor(initial$inflation, initial$UNRATE))`, so that scatter alone
does not tell us whether unemployment improves forecasts.

```{r}
#| label: fig-initial
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-cap: "Initial-sample time plots and ACFs. Lag is measured in quarters; dashed ACF bands are approximate 95% white-noise bounds."
par(mfrow = c(3, 2), mar = c(3.1, 3.6, 2.1, 0.8), mgp = c(2, 0.65, 0),
    cex = 0.78)
for (j in seq_along(series)) {
  y <- initial[[series[j]]]
  plot(ts(y, start = c(1960, 1), frequency = 4), ylab = "Percent",
       xlab = "", main = series_names[j], col = "#246B8E", lwd = 1)
  acf(y, lag.max = 24, main = "", xlab = "Lag (quarters)")
  title(main = "ACF", line = 0.5, font.main = 1)
}
```

\newpage

# Step 1: Stationarity and structural change

All three series are persistent in @fig-initial. Their lag-1 autocorrelations are
`r paste(sprintf("%.2f", sapply(initial[series], function(y) acf(y, plot = FALSE)$acf[2])), collapse = ", ")`,
respectively. Inflation and the bill rate show particularly large changes around
the high-inflation period; unemployment moves through long cycles, including its
early-1980s peak. None looks well described by one straight deterministic trend.

We therefore use an intercept but no linear trend in each ADF regression, and
level-stationarity KPSS tests. The ADF null is a unit root; the KPSS null is
stationarity around a constant. We compare both tests at 5%. For ADF, we select
0-4 augmentation lags by BIC on a common sample, then refit the selected lag
using all available rows. For KPSS, we use the short bandwidth, which is four
lags here. The same choices apply to first differences.

```{r}
#| label: stationarity-tests
test_series <- function(y) {
  differences <- embed(diff(y), 5)
  regression_data <- data.frame(change = differences[, 1],
                                level = y[5:(length(y) - 1)], differences[, 2:5])
  names(regression_data)[3:6] <- paste0("lag", 1:4)
  bic <- sapply(0:4, function(k) {
    formula <- reformulate(c("level", head(paste0("lag", 1:4), k)),
                           response = "change")
    BIC(lm(formula, data = regression_data))
  })
  k <- which.min(bic) - 1
  adf <- ur.df(y, type = "drift", lags = k, selectlags = "Fixed")
  kpss <- ur.kpss(y, type = "mu", lags = "short")
  data.frame(ADF_lags = k, ADF = adf@teststat[1, "tau2"],
             KPSS = kpss@teststat, KPSS_lags = kpss@lag)
}
tests <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(series), function(j) {
  y <- initial[[series[j]]]
  rbind(cbind(Series = series_names[j], Form = "Level", test_series(y)),
        cbind(Series = series_names[j], Form = "First difference", test_series(diff(y))))
}))
knitr::kable(tests[c("Series", "Form", "ADF_lags", "ADF", "KPSS")],
             col.names = c("Series", "Form", "ADF lags", "ADF", "KPSS"),
             digits = 3, booktabs = TRUE)
```

The 5% critical values are -2.880 for ADF and 0.463 for KPSS. Reject the ADF
null for a more negative statistic, and the KPSS null for a larger statistic.
At levels, ADF does not reject a unit root for any series, while KPSS rejects
constant-mean stationarity for all three. After one difference, ADF rejects and
KPSS does not reject for every series.

| Series | ADF evidence | KPSS evidence | Structural-change evidence | Classification |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| CPI inflation | Reject only after differencing | Reject only in levels | Changing mean and variability | $I(1)$, provisionally |
| Unemployment | Reject only after differencing | Reject only in levels | Long cycles; early-1980s peak | $I(1)$, provisionally |
| T-bill rate | Reject only after differencing | Reject only in levels | Early-1980s peak, then decline | $I(1)$, provisionally |

These are working classifications, not proof of a permanent unit root. A changing
mean can make stationary behavior within periods look nonstationary over the full
sample, and the tests do not separate those explanations. The project still calls
for its specified forecasting models; we do not replace them with differenced
models solely because of these tests. The changing inflation mean gives a reason
to compare the gap models with fixed-mean alternatives.

# Step 2: Expanding-window forecast setup

The first forecast origin is 1999Q4, using 1960Q1-1999Q4 for estimation.
At each later origin, we add one quarter, re-estimate the model, and retain
forecasts at horizons 1, 4, and 8. The final historical target is 2019Q4;
observations from 2020 onward are reserved for the later project stage.

The shared evaluation harness, `R/02_harness.R`, runs every model through this design.

```{r}
#| label: code-harness
#| file: R/02_harness.R
```

```{r}
#| label: forecast-schedule
first_origin <- match("1999Q4", panel$quarter)
last_target <- match("2019Q4", panel$quarter)
schedule <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 4, 8), function(h) {
  origins <- first_origin:(last_target - h)
  data.frame(origin = panel$quarter[origins],
             target_quarter = panel$quarter[origins + h],
             horizon = h, training_quarters = origins)
}))
stopifnot(identical(as.integer(table(schedule$horizon)), c(80L, 77L, 73L)),
          !anyDuplicated(schedule[c("origin", "horizon")]))
schedule_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(schedule, schedule$horizon), function(x) {
  data.frame(Horizon = x$horizon[1], `First origin` = x$origin[1],
             `Last origin` = tail(x$origin, 1), `First target` = x$target_quarter[1],
             `Last target` = tail(x$target_quarter, 1), Errors = nrow(x),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))
knitr::kable(schedule_summary, row.names = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE)
```

The schedule contains 230 origin-horizon pairs per model. The counts differ
because a forecast made eight quarters ahead reaches its first target later
than a one-quarter forecast. Within each horizon, all seven models must use
the same target quarters.

## Estimation and data boundaries

At origin $T$, only observations through $T$ enter fitting, lag selection, or
smoothing. For the direct AR and direct Phillips-curve models, the response is
$\pi_{t+h}$, so a training row is usable only when $t+h\leq T$. Each horizon gets
its own regression and BIC lag selection over 1-4 inflation lags. Candidate
lag orders should be compared on the same available response rows.

Variables, transformations, candidate lag ranges, estimation methods, horizons,
and forecast construction stay fixed throughout evaluation; only fitted
parameters and BIC-selected lag orders are updated at each origin. Later forecast
errors must not be used to revise those choices.

For example, at origin 1999Q4 with $h=4$, the latest training row is dated
1998Q4 and its response is inflation in 1999Q4. The new forecast uses regressors
observed in 1999Q4 to predict inflation in 2000Q4. The Phillips-curve model adds
unemployment observed at the regressor date, not future unemployment.

The source files contain revised historical observations rather than real-time
vintages, so
the experiment is pseudo-out-of-sample, not a reconstruction of the information
actually released at each historical date.

## Shared output for the model comparison

Each model function returns a tibble with `h` and `forecast`, as required
by the shared harness. The harness adds `model`, `origin`, `target`, `actual`, and
`error = actual - forecast`. Positive errors mean underprediction. Every model
passes its forecast-count check. The saved forecasts contain 230 rows per
model, with no missing or duplicate origin-horizon pairs.

\newpage

# Step 3: Core forecasting models

Each model's functions live in its owner's file in `R/`, shown below in full.

## Model 1: Random walk

At forecast origin $T$, we generate point forecasts using a random walk
model without drift:

$$ \pi_{t} = \pi_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad E(\varepsilon_t) = 0, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_t) = \sigma_\varepsilon^2 $$

The $h$-step-ahead point forecast is set to the most recent observed
inflation rate:

$$ \widehat{\pi}_{T+h \mid T}^{\mathrm{RW}} = \pi_T $$

The function verifies that the training sample contains valid finite
observations and repeats this value to produce point forecasts for
horizons $h \in \{1, 4, 8\}$. No estimation or iteration is required.

## Model 2: Four-quarter-average benchmark

At forecast origin $T$, we compute point forecasts as the sample average
of the four most recently observed inflation rates:

$$ \widehat{\pi}_{T+h \mid T}^{\mathrm{4Q}} = \frac{1}{4} \sum_{j=0}^{3} \pi_{T-j} $$

The function verifies that the training sample contains at least four
finite observations, extracts the four most recent values, and
calculates their mean $\bar{\pi}_T$. This single value is then assigned
as the point forecast across horizons $h \in \{1, 4, 8\}$.

```{r}
#| label: code-models-chandra
#| file: R/03_models_chandra.R
```

## Model 3: AR(p)

At each forecast origin $T$, we estimate an autoregressive model with an intercept for next-quarter inflation:

$$\pi_t = c + \sum_{j=1}^p \phi_j \pi_{t-j} + \varepsilon_t$$

Candidate lag orders $p \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ are evaluated using BIC on a common sample starting at the fifth training quarter ($t=5$), ensuring that each candidate order model is compared over an identical set of response observations. We then refit the selected order on all available historical rows for that $p$ .

Point forecasts through horizon $h=8$ are generated iteratively using the same estimated coefficients:

$$\widehat{\pi}_{T+k \mid T} = c + \sum_{j=1}^p \phi_j \widehat{\pi}_{T+k-j \mid T}, \quad k = 1, \dots, 8,$$

where unobserved future values are replaced by earlier iterative forecasts. If stationary, the model implies a fixed long-run mean $\mu = c / (1 - \sum \phi_j)$. The code in `R/03_models_jana.R` provides `model_ar(train)` for and `fit_ar(train)`.

## Local mean by simple exponential smoothing

Following Faust and Wright (2013, Section 4.4.5), we construct a time-varying local mean $\tau_t$ using simple exponential smoothing with a fixed parameter $\alpha = 0.05$ (95% weight on the previous local mean and 5% weight on current inflation):

$$\tau_{1960Q1} = \pi_{1960Q1}, \qquad \tau_t = 0.95 \tau_{t-1} + 0.05 \pi_t \quad (t > 1).$$

The calculation is strictly one-sided: at origin $T$, the local mean $\tau_T$ depends only on inflation observed through quarter $T$ and uses no future observations. The inflation gap $g_t$ measures the deviation of observed inflation from this slow-moving trend:

$$g_t = \pi_t - \tau_t.$$

This transformation is implemented in `calc_local_mean(infl, alpha = 0.05)` and serves as the foundation for Models 5 and 6.

## Model 5: Gap AR

The gap AR model recenters inflation around the slow-moving local mean by estimating an autoregression on the stationary inflation gap $g_t$:

$$g_t = a + \sum_{j=1}^p \rho_j g_{t-j} + v_t.$$

At each origin $T$, lag length $p \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ is selected by BIC on the common sample ($t=5, \dots, T$) and refit on all available historical gap observations, similar to the procedure described for Model 3. Forecasts of the gap $\widehat{g}_{T+h \mid T}$ are generated iteratively through eight quarters.

The future local mean is held constant at $\tau_T$, as future inflation rates needed to update it are not yet available. The final inflation forecast adds the origin local mean back to the gap forecast:

$$\widehat{\pi}^{GAP}_{T+h \mid T} = \tau_T + \widehat{g}_{T+h \mid T}.$$

Comparison with the standard AR($p$) model examines whether filtering out low-frequency shifts in trend inflation improves forecast accuracy. The model is implemented in `model_gap_ar(train)` and `fit_gap_ar(train)`.

## Model 6: Fixed-persistence gap forecast

Model 6 adopts the restricted specification from Faust and Wright (2013, Section 4.4.7), which eliminates parameter estimation uncertainty by imposing a fixed persistence value of 0.46:

$$\widehat{\pi}^{FIX}_{T+h \mid T} = \tau_T + 0.46^h g_T.$$

Here, $g_T = \pi_T - \tau_T$ is the inflation gap observed at origin $T$. As the forecast horizon $h$ extends, the gap component decays geometrically ($0.46^1 = 0.46$, $0.46^4 \approx 0.045$, $0.46^8 \approx 0.002$), smoothly pulling the forecast back toward the current local mean $\tau_T$.

In this model no parameters are estimated, eliminating sample estimation error entirely. Comparing Model 6 with Model 5 tests whether estimating additional persistence parameters provides sufficient forecasting benefit to compensate for parameter estimation uncertainty. This model is implemented in `model_gap_fixed(train)`.

```{r}
#| label: code-models-jana
#| file: R/03_models_jana.R
```

## Model 4: Direct AR

For each horizon $h=1,4,8$, we fit a separate regression with an intercept:

$$
\pi_{t+h}=c_h+\sum_{j=0}^{p_h-1}\phi_{h,j}\pi_{t-j}+\varepsilon_{t+h}.
$$

At origin $T$, the final response in estimation is $\pi_T$, so the most recent
regressor row is dated $T-h$. BIC selects $p_h$ from 1 through 4 on a common
sample beginning at the fourth training quarter. We then refit the selected order
on all rows available for that order. The forecast uses inflation at $T$ and its
selected lags. No iterative forecasts or future inflation regressors are used.

## Model 7: Direct Phillips curve

The Phillips-curve model adds unemployment observed at each regressor date:

$$
\pi_{t+h}=c_h+\sum_{j=0}^{p_h-1}\phi_{h,j}\pi_{t-j}
+\lambda_h u_t+\varepsilon_{t+h}.
$$

It has its own BIC lag selection at each horizon and origin, using the same
candidate orders and sample rule as the direct AR. Forecasting uses $u_T$,
not unemployment at $T+h$. Both models stay in levels, as the guide specifies.

The code in `R/03_models_odysseus.R` supplies `direct_ar_model(train)` and
`phillips_model(train)`. The small shared fitting function keeps their response
alignment and lag-selection rules identical.

```{r}
#| label: code-models-odysseus
#| file: R/03_models_odysseus.R
```

## Running all models

All seven models run through the shared harness in one place. The list below gives the labels used in
every results table. All seven functions must be available before running the comparison.

```{r}
#| label: run-all-models
#| results: hide
model_fns <- c(
  "Random walk"    = "model_rw",
  "4Q average"     = "model_4q",
  "AR(p)"          = "model_ar",
  "Direct AR"      = "direct_ar_model",
  "Gap AR"         = "model_gap_ar",
  "Fixed gap"      = "model_gap_fixed",
  "Phillips curve" = "phillips_model"
)
stopifnot(all(vapply(model_fns, exists, logical(1))))
models <- lapply(model_fns, get)

results <- run_harness(q, models)
check_counts(results)

# frozen forecasts: saved once, before any evaluation
dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
results |>
  mutate(across(c(origin, target), format)) |>
  write.csv("results/forecasts.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: first-origin
train_1999 <- q |> as_tibble() |> filter(qtr <= yearquarter("1999 Q4"))
first_fc <- results |>
  filter(origin == yearquarter("1999 Q4"),
         model %in% c("Direct AR", "Phillips curve")) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(p = fit_direct(train_1999, h, unemployment = model == "Phillips curve")$p) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(target = format(target)) |>
  select(model, h, target, p, forecast)
knitr::kable(first_fc, digits = 3, booktabs = TRUE,
             col.names = c("Model", "Horizon", "Target", "Lags", "Forecast"),
             caption = "Forecasts from the first origin, 1999Q4 (annualized percent).")
```

The target is inflation in the indicated single quarter, not average or cumulative
inflation over the next $h$ quarters. Coefficients and selected lag orders are
updated as the estimation window expands; the model definitions do not change.

# Step 4: Forecast evaluation

## Comparison of all seven models


We use the saved forecasts in `results` from Step 3, without fitting the models
again. All models have the same target quarters within each horizon: 80 at
$h=1$, 77 at $h=4$, and 73 at $h=8$, following the schedule in Step 2.
With $e_t=\pi_t-\hat\pi_t$, we calculate
$\mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\operatorname{mean}(e_t^2)}$,
$\mathrm{MAE}=\operatorname{mean}(|e_t|)$, and
$\mathrm{ME}=\operatorname{mean}(e_t)$. These are in percentage points of
annualized inflation; negative mean error indicates overprediction.
Relative RMSE divides a model's RMSE by the four-quarter-average RMSE at
the same horizon. RMSE is the primary ranking measure.

```{r}
#| label: code-evaluation-odysseus
#| file: R/04_evaluation_odysseus.R
```

```{r}
#| label: step4-scores
scores <- evaluate_forecasts(results, benchmark = "4Q average")
write.csv(scores, "results/scores.csv", row.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(scores, digits = 3, booktabs = TRUE,
  col.names = c("Model", "h", "n", "RMSE", "Relative RMSE", "MAE", "Mean error"),
  caption = "Forecast accuracy for all seven models, ordered by RMSE within horizon.")
```

Relative RMSE below one indicates lower RMSE than the four-quarter average.

## Results by horizon

At $h=1$, fixed gap has the lowest RMSE (3.002), followed by the four-quarter average (3.039). Their MAEs both round to 1.873, with the four-quarter average slightly lower before rounding. AR(p) and direct AR give identical one-step forecasts, as expected from their matching regression and lag-selection rules at this horizon. The Phillips curve has slightly higher RMSE and MAE than direct AR.

At $h=4$, fixed gap again has the lowest RMSE and MAE (2.726 and 1.617), followed by gap AR. The 4Q average ranks third in performance at $h=4$. Iterated AR(p) does better than direct AR, while adding unemployment to direct AR does not improve either error measure.

At $h=8$, fixed gap remains lowest on both measures (RMSE 2.781; MAE 1.688),
with gap AR second. All seven models overpredict on average. The mean errors
are -0.370 and -0.430 for the two gap models, compared with -1.440 for direct AR
and -1.553 for the Phillips curve.

Fixed gap has the lowest RMSE at every horizon, with relative RMSE of 0.988,
0.933, and 0.912. Gap AR also beats the four-quarter average at horizons 4 and 8,
but not at horizon 1. The random walk has the highest RMSE at every horizon.
These are descriptive rankings, not significance tests.
The Phillips-curve result applies to this specification and sample, not to the
usefulness of unemployment in general. Different horizons have different target
periods, so lower RMSE at a longer horizon does not imply that forecasting
further ahead is easier.

```{r}
#| label: step4-plot-setup
plot_data <- scores |>
  select(model, h, RMSE, MAE) |>
  pivot_longer(c(RMSE, MAE), names_to = "Metric", values_to = "Error") |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = rev(names(models))))
accuracy_plot <- function(horizon) {
  ggplot(filter(plot_data, h == horizon),
         aes(Error, model, colour = Metric, shape = Metric)) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(MAE = "#4477AA", RMSE = "#AA3377")) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, ceiling(max(plot_data$Error)))) +
    labs(x = "Error (percentage points of annualized inflation)", y = NULL,
         title = paste0("h = ", horizon,
                        if (horizon == 1) " quarter ahead" else " quarters ahead")) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(face = "plain"))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-step4-h1
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "One-quarter-ahead accuracy on the common 80-quarter target sample."
accuracy_plot(1)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-step4-h4
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "Four-quarter-ahead accuracy on the common 77-quarter target sample."
accuracy_plot(4)
```

\newpage

```{r}
#| label: fig-step4-h8
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "Eight-quarter-ahead accuracy on the common 73-quarter target sample."
accuracy_plot(8)
```

The plots share a horizontal scale. RMSE and MAE give the same model ordering
except for the nearly tied fixed-gap and four-quarter-average MAEs at $h=1$.
The one-step AR(p)/direct AR tie holds for both measures. RMSE exceeds MAE
for every model, reflecting its greater weight on large errors. The largest
absolute forecast error occurs in 2008Q4, except for the random walk at $h=8$,
whose largest error is in 2010Q4. The 2008Q4 observation remains in the main
comparison; the sensitivity check in Step 5 does
not change the assigned evaluation sample.

\newpage

# Step 5: Diagnostics for the leading one-step model

Step 5 checks the residuals of the leading one-step model. We look for
remaining autocorrelation, unstable variability, and large errors that may
drive RMSE. As the guide specifies, we select the estimated core model with
the lowest $h=1$ RMSE. The random-walk, four-quarter-average, and fixed-gap
forecasts are excluded because they estimate no parameters.

```{r}
#| label: step5-select
# lowest h = 1 RMSE among the estimated core models
h1_rmse <- results |>
  filter(h == 1 & model %in% c("AR(p)", "Direct AR", "Gap AR", "Phillips curve")) |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarize(rmse = sqrt(mean(error^2))) |>
  arrange(rmse)
h1_rmse

best_model <- h1_rmse |> slice(1) |> pull(model)
best_model
```

The gap AR has the lowest one-step RMSE, `r sprintf("%.2f", h1_rmse$rmse[1])`.
AR(p) and the direct AR follow at `r sprintf("%.2f", h1_rmse$rmse[2])`; they
produce identical one-step forecasts.

We refit the gap AR on all data through 2019Q4. The local mean is rebuilt
from this sample, and BIC again selects the gap lag order.

```{r}
#| label: step5-refit
# guard: stop if a different model wins the h = 1 comparison
stopifnot(best_model == "Gap AR")

# all data through 2019Q4
train_2019 <- q |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(qtr <= yearquarter("2019 Q4")) |>
  select(qtr, infl, unrate, tbill)

gap_fit <- fit_gap_ar(train_2019)

gap_fit$p
summary(gap_fit$fit)
```

BIC selects `r gap_fit$p` gap lags. The lag coefficients sum to
`r sprintf("%.2f", sum(coef(gap_fit$fit)[-1]))`, so the gap is persistent but
reverts toward the local mean. The intercept is near zero, as expected for a
deviation from the local mean. The residual standard error is
`r sprintf("%.2f", sigma(gap_fit$fit))` percentage points across
`r nrow(gap_fit$resid)` residuals.

@fig-step5-resid plots the refit residuals. Well-specified residuals should
vary around zero without trends or long runs.

```{r}
#| label: fig-step5-resid
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "Gap AR residuals, refit through 2019Q4 (percentage points)."
resid_ts <- gap_fit$resid |> as_tsibble(index = qtr)

resid_ts |>
  autoplot(resid) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Residual (pp)")
```
```{r}
#| label: step5-largest
# five largest residuals in absolute value
largest <- resid_ts |>
  as_tibble() |>
  slice_max(abs(resid), n = 5) |>
  mutate(qtr = format(qtr), resid = round(resid, 2))
knitr::kable(largest, col.names = c("Quarter", "Residual"), booktabs = TRUE)
```

The residuals center on zero with no visible trend. The largest errors are
2008Q4, 2005Q3, 2005Q4, 1986Q1, and 1981Q4. Most coincide with energy-price
shocks: the late-2008 oil collapse, the 2005 gasoline spike and reversal, and
the 1986 oil-price drop. 1981Q4 falls during the Volcker disinflation. Their
spread also changes over time, with wider swings in the 1970s to mid-1980s
and after 2005 than in between.

@fig-step5-acf shows the residual autocorrelations. A Ljung-Box test checks
whether the first eight are jointly zero, with degrees of freedom reduced by
the `r gap_fit$p` estimated lag coefficients.

```{r}
#| label: fig-step5-acf
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "Gap AR residual ACF through 20 quarters. Dashed lines are approximate 95% bounds."
resid_ts |>
  ACF(resid, lag_max = 20) |>
  autoplot() +
  labs(x = "Lag (quarters)", y = "ACF")

lb <- resid_ts |> features(resid, ljung_box, lag = 8, dof = gap_fit$p)
lb
```

All 20 autocorrelations fall inside the approximate bounds, and lags 1 to 3
are close to zero. The Ljung-Box statistic is
`r sprintf("%.2f", lb$lb_stat)` with `r 8 - gap_fit$p` degrees of freedom
(p = `r sprintf("%.3f", lb$lb_pvalue)`), so we do not reject the null of no
autocorrelation through lag 8. For comparison, inflation itself has a lag-1
autocorrelation of about 0.75 over 1960Q1-1999Q4. The gap AR removes that
persistence from its errors.

Next we check whether the size of the errors is stable. @fig-step5-sd shows
a trailing 20-quarter standard deviation of the residuals, and the table
below compares the residual standard deviation across periods.

```{r}
#| label: fig-step5-sd
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "Trailing 20-quarter standard deviation of the gap AR residuals (percentage points)."
resid_ts <- resid_ts |>
  mutate(roll_sd = slide_dbl(resid, sd, .before = 19, .complete = TRUE))

resid_ts |>
  autoplot(roll_sd) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "SD (pp)")
```


```{r}
#| label: step5-sd-period
sd_by_period <- resid_ts |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(period = case_when(
    qtr <= yearquarter("1972 Q4") ~ "1960-1972",
    qtr <= yearquarter("1986 Q4") ~ "1973-1986",
    qtr <= yearquarter("2004 Q4") ~ "1987-2004",
    TRUE ~ "2005-2019")) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarize(quarters = n(), sd = sd(resid), max_abs = max(abs(resid)))
knitr::kable(sd_by_period, digits = 2, booktabs = TRUE,
             col.names = c("Period", "Quarters", "Residual SD", "Largest |residual|"))
```

The residual standard deviation is not constant. It is about
`r sprintf("%.1f", sd_by_period$sd[1])` in 1960-1972 and
`r sprintf("%.1f", sd_by_period$sd[3])` in 1987-2004, but
`r sprintf("%.1f", sd_by_period$sd[2])` in 1973-1986 and
`r sprintf("%.1f", sd_by_period$sd[4])` in 2005-2019. The flat peak from 2008
to 2013 in @fig-step5-sd comes from 2008Q4 alone: it raises the trailing
standard deviation until it leaves the 20-quarter window.

```{r}
#| label: step5-influence
gap_h1 <- results |> filter(model == "Gap AR", h == 1)
influence <- tibble(
  Measure = c("RMSE, all 80 targets", "RMSE, excluding 2008Q4", "MAE, all 80 targets"),
  Value = c(sqrt(mean(gap_h1$error^2)),
            sqrt(mean(gap_h1$error[gap_h1$target != yearquarter("2008 Q4")]^2)),
            mean(abs(gap_h1$error))))
knitr::kable(influence, digits = 2, booktabs = TRUE)
```

The out-of-sample forecast errors show the same sensitivity. Dropping 2008Q4,
one of 80 targets, lowers the gap AR's one-step RMSE from
`r sprintf("%.2f", influence$Value[1])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", influence$Value[2])`.
Its MAE is `r sprintf("%.2f", influence$Value[3])`, well below RMSE.

Overall, the gap AR leaves no detectable autocorrelation in its errors, but
their variance changes across periods and a few energy-driven shocks dominate
its RMSE. Small RMSE differences between models in Step 4 should therefore be
read with care.

# Step 6: Summary

Based on the Step 4 results:

- Lowest-RMSE model by horizon: The Fixed gap model achieves the lowest
  RMSE across all three evaluation horizons ($h=1$: 3.002, $h=4$: 2.726,
  $h=8$: 2.781).

- Models outperforming the benchmark: At $h=1$, only the Fixed gap model
  achieves a lower RMSE than the four-quarter-average benchmark. At
  $h=4$ and $h=8$, both the Fixed gap and Gap AR models achieve lower
  RMSEs than the four-quarter-average benchmark.

- Main patterns in MAE and Mean Error: MAE closely tracks the RMSE model
  rankings at each horizon, with the lowest MAE occurring at $h=4$. Mean
  error is negative across almost all models and horizons—worsening
  significantly at longer horizons—indicating persistent systemic
  overprediction of inflation during the evaluation period.
